# facett_icebergview - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-icebergview/0.1.10/facett_icebergview/

## Expand description

**facett-icebergview** — browse **and time-travel** one Iceberg table, drawn
from **Arrow  RecordBatches**. The component is

*engine-agnostic*: you hand it, per Iceberg snapshot, the snapshot’s metadata + its materialized Arrow frame; it renders a

**snapshot picker**(newest-first, showing snapshot id / timestamp / row-count) over a virtualized,

**paged**row grid (the rows come from

[, built from the batch via](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[). Selecting a snapshot loads](https://docs.rs/facett-arrow/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_arrow/index.html)

`facett_arrow`*that*snapshot’s frame — time travel.

Like every facett component it implements [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html) (

`title` / `ui` /
`state_json`), so it drops into a `FacetDeck` and is robot-testable through
`facett_core::harness`: drive [/](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.select_snapshot)

`IcebergView::select_snapshot`[headlessly and assert](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.set_page)

`IcebergView::set_page``state_json` (the current snapshot, the snapshot list,
and the visible rows all change). `state_json` exposes:- `table`— the table name,
- `snapshots`— every snapshot newest-first (- `id`,- `timestamp_ms`,- `rows`),
- `current`— the selected snapshot id,
- `total_rows`/- `page`/- `page_size`/- `visible_rows`— the paged view.

**Why not just  facett-table?** A table viewer shows

*one*frame. This adds the Iceberg dimension — the history of snapshots and the control to scrub between them — which is the whole point of a lakehouse table browser. The adapter that

*fills*it from a real catalog (skade) lives host-side (korp / nornir) so this crate never takes a hard catalog/engine dependency.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Iceberg](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html)- View
- A browse + time-travel viewer for one Iceberg table.
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.Snapshot.html)
- One snapshot paired with the Arrow frame that materializes it. The frame is a
`Vec<RecordBatch>`exactly as a scan returns it;`IcebergView`concatenates the rows into a paged`Table`
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.SnapshotMeta.html)- Meta
- One Iceberg snapshot’s identity, for the picker + `state_json`. Mirrors what`iceberg::spec::Snapshot`exposes (`snapshot_id()`/`timestamp_ms()`) plus a row count the host computes (scan count, or the snapshot summary’s`total-records`).

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE.html)- PAGE_ - SIZE
- Default rows shown per page (the Table is virtualized, but paging keeps a huge
snapshot from being cell-formatted all at once and makes `visible_rows`meaningful for headless assertions).

# facett_warehousedeck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-warehousedeck/0.1.10/facett_warehousedeck/

## Expand description

**facett-warehousedeck** — a multi-pane **dashboard over a lakehouse
warehouse**. It views the warehouse as **many components at once**: several
**3D graphs** (call graph, dependency graph, world-delta, release lineage,
SBOM/vuln) **plus** grids and charts, all visible simultaneously in a wall.

It is built **entirely from existing facett widgets** — it never reimplements
a viewer. Each pane is one of:
[ facett_graph3d::Graph3D](https://docs.rs/facett-graph3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_graph3d/struct.Graph3D.html) ·

[/](https://docs.rs/facett-grid/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_grid/struct.Grid.html)

`facett_grid::Grid`[·](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[, composed inside a](https://docs.rs/facett-plot/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_plot/struct.PlotView.html)

`facett_plot::PlotView`[. The deck is rendered in](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html)

`FacetDeck::wall_ui``Graph3D` instances) draws at once; a **Focus**mode falls back to the deck’s tabbed

[.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.ui)

Like the rest of facett, this crate takes **data, not a catalog**: a host

# sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer-riemann/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann/

## Expand description

Neo-Riemannian / functional triad naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate implements the Riemannian naming school: it labels a triad by its
functional quality relative to its root, distinguishing a major triad (`T`,
upper-case for the major tonic function) from a minor triad (`t`,
lower-case). [ label_riemann](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html) rotates the pitch-class set so the root sits at
zero and matches the major or minor triad signature; non-triadic sets return

`None`.## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [label_](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html)- riemann
- Labels `mask`as a major (`T`) or minor (`t`) triad relative to its root.

# facett_security - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-security/0.1.10/facett_security/

## Expand description

**facett-security** — a software-supply-chain **security report** view: the
**verdict** (Pass / Warn / Block), the **findings** list (id · severity ·
package · advisory · fix) with **severity / EPSS / KEV** columns, and a
secondary **CVE / advisory** reference table. It is the UI *twin* of
[modgunn](https://codeberg.org/nordisk/modgunn)’s scan output — the gate that
decides whether an artifact may be served / promoted.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-on-purpose-no-modgunn-dependency)Generic on purpose (no modgunn dependency)

facett MUST NOT couple to the modgunn crate. So this crate carries its **own**
plain, serializable structs — [ Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)

`Severity`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)

`Finding`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)

`Artifact`[— whose shape](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)

`SecurityReport`**mirrors**so a consumer (nornir-viz / holger-ui) maps the two

`modgunn::core`**1:1**with no glue:

| facett-security | modgunn::core |
|---|---|
| (Pass/Warn/Block)`Verdict` | `Decision`(Pass/Warn/Block) — same`Ord` |
| (Info…Critical)`Severity` | `Severity`(Info…Critical) — same`Ord` |
| `Finding``{id,severity,…}` | `Finding``{id,severity,summary}`(superset) |
| `Artifact` | `ArtifactRef` |
| `SecurityReport` | `Verdict`(the whole cacheable result) |

[ Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html) is a

**superset**: modgunn’s three fields map straight in, and the richer scan columns the UI wants (

`package`, `advisory`, `fix`, `epss`, `kev`)
are optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has and leaves the rest defaulted.[§](https://docs.rs#fc-compliance-the-component-contract)FC compliance (the component contract)

- **FC-1 / FC-3**— all observable state lives in one serializable- `SecurityState`- `Serialize`/- `Deserialize`/- `Clone`/- `PartialEq`), read back via- `SecurityView::state`
- **FC-2 / FC-9**— every input is a- `Msg`- `SecurityView::update`- `render`- `&self`that paints and- *returns*the- `Msg`- `Facet::ui`
- **FC-4**— the painted verdict pill emits an AccessKit node; every finding row / CVE row is a selectable, labelled, value-carrying node.
- **FC-5**— rows are keyed off the finding- **id**(a stable domain key), never a loop index.
- **FC-6**— pure egui + painter, renders headlessly (the deck robot path).
- **FC-7**— no ambient clock / RNG / animation: the scan time is an- *injected*host-stamped string (- `SecurityReport::scanned_at`
- **FC-8**— the view does no I/O;- `SecurityView::is_idle`- `SecurityView::update`- `Vec<Effect>`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)
- The artifact a verdict is about (content-addressed). Mirrors
`modgunn::core::ArtifactRef`.
- [Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)
- One thing the scanner found. `id`,`severity`,`summary`map straight from`modgunn::core::Finding`; the rest are the richer scan columns the UI shows (all optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has).
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)- Report
- The cacheable scan result: the verdict + its findings + the keys it was
computed against. The plain data a host hands the view; mirrors the whole of
`modgunn::core::Verdict`.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityState.html)- State
- **All**observable state for the view (FC-1 / FC-3): the report plus the UI state (the drilled-in finding, the severity floor filter, and the zoom). Fully serializable so a caller reads it back at any frame boundary.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityView.html)- View
- The `Facet``SecurityReport`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Effect](https://docs.rs/enum.Effect.html)
- Side work as data (FC-8). The view does no I/O, so this is uninhabited — it exists to make the “no pending effects” contract explicit and type-checked.
- [Msg](https://docs.rs/enum.Msg.html)
- Every input the view accepts (FC-2). The **only**legal way to mutate`SecurityState``Debug`+`Clone`.
- [Severity](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)
- Finding severity (declaration order = ascending, so the worst finding is the
`max()`). Mirrors`modgunn::core::Severity`.
- [Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html)
- What a gate should DO with the artifact, given the findings. Declaration
order is the strictness order — `Pass < Warn < Block`— so folding many findings into one verdict is their`Ord::max``modgunn::core::Decision`relies on).

# facett_plandag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-plandag/0.1.10/facett_plandag/

## Expand description

**facett-plandag** — a **metric-bearing operator DAG**: the Spark **SQL query
plan** / Databricks **Query Profile graph**. Each node carries a multi-line
**metric body** (time / memory / rows / spill); a **cost-heat** switch
(Time / Memory / Rows) fills nodes by relative cost; **WholeStageCodegen groups**
collapse into super-nodes; and an **AQE initial-vs-final** toggle flips between
the two plan versions. The four things the doc says no single facett graph had
at once.

It **composes** facett’s existing graph stack — exactly the documented “compose
`facett_graph`, paint our own” pattern:

- `facett_graph::DepGraphView`- **column layering**+- `facett_graph::draw_arrow`
- [`facett_pipeline::Status`] supplies the**themed node-status colour**.
- The pure, serializable `model`

[§](https://docs.rs#fc-contract)FC contract

- **Serializable state**(- `state_json`): the resolved graph (every node’s metric body + its- **cost-heat as DATA**), the active metric/version, the collapse set, the selection.
- `Msg`- `PlanDagView::update`
- **Render-proof**: the painter and- `state_json`both read from one- `model::resolve`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use model::`- [CostMetric](https://docs.rs/model/enum.CostMetric.html);
- `pub use model::`- [Metrics](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Metrics.html);
- `pub use model::`- [OpStatus](https://docs.rs/model/enum.OpStatus.html);

# facett_helix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-helix/0.1.10/facett_helix/

## Expand description

**facett-helix** — the **TIME-HELIX DAG view**. A plan / dependency DAG rendered
as a **helix that advances ALONG a time axis**: each node is a plan item (idea /
task / test / crate) tied to a `system` (its angular lane / strand); the DAG winds
*forward through time* rather than spinning in place. Edges are **soft rounded
rubberband splines** (Catmull-Rom, elastic settle); coils can be **wound onto a
pin** (`wind`); many coils coexist in one scene with **inter-helix links**; an
**animated traverse** flies a time-cursor along the axis. GPU-rendered with the
emissive **bloom** lane reused from `facett-graph3d`.

[§](https://docs.rs#portability-contract-the-reason-this-crate-exists)Portability contract (the reason this crate exists)

[ model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html) +

[depend on](https://docs.rs/layout/index.html)

`layout`**nothing but**— no egui, no facett, no nornir/modgunn. They are the seam that

`serde` + `std``git mv`s into **ordning**. Only

[(this file) binds to facett’s](https://docs.rs/struct.HelixView.html)

`HelixView`[/egui/](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet``facett-graph3d`. Hosts
(nornir’s funnel, modgunn) just *populate*a

[through the](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Scene.html)

`model::Scene`[API; facett stays generic.](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanDag.html#method.add_idea)

`model::PlanDag::add_idea`[§](https://docs.rs#fc-contract)FC contract

- **Serializable state**(- `state_json`- `t`, angular lane, system) + the wind / level / cursor / tension — the picture asserted as DATA.
- `Msg`- `update`
- **Injected clock**(- `set_clock`- `Msg::Tick`
- **AccessKit**: each node rides into the tree as a queryable Button (FC-4).

# everruns_a2ui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-a2ui/0.17.3/everruns_a2ui/

## Expand description

A2UI component catalog and prompt generator for Everruns.

Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to emit A2UI JSON component trees. The JSON is transported in ```a2ui fenced code blocks and rendered by the UI using native shadcn/ui primitives.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_a2ui::{PromptOptions, default_catalog, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_catalog(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```a2ui"));
```
Ref: specs/a2ui.md
Ref: [https://github.com/google/a2ui](https://github.com/google/a2ui)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Catalog](https://docs.rs/struct.Catalog.html)
- A catalog describes the components an agent may emit.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentCategory.html)- Category
- One category of components in a catalog (e.g. “Layout”, “Forms”).
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentDef.html)- Def
- One component available to the agent.
- [Prompt](https://docs.rs/struct.PromptOptions.html)- Options
- Options for customizing the generated prompt.
- [PropDef](https://docs.rs/struct.PropDef.html)
- One prop of a component.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_catalog.html)- catalog
- The default A2UI catalog.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_prompt.html)- prompt
- Generate the default A2UI system prompt with standard options.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_prompt.html)- prompt
- Build the full A2UI system prompt.

# everruns_openui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-openui/0.17.3/everruns_openui/

## Expand description

OpenUI component library and prompt generator for Everruns.

Rust reimplementation of the OpenUI component definitions and prompt generator. Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to generate OpenUI Lang code.

The generated prompt is compatible with `@openuidev/react-lang` and `@openuidev/react-ui`
— the React runtime parses the LLM output and renders it into interactive components.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_openui::{PromptOptions, default_library, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_library(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```openui"));
```
Ref: [https://github.com/thesysdev/openui](https://github.com/thesysdev/openui)

- Component definitions: packages/react-ui/src/genui-lib/
- Prompt generator: packages/react-lang/src/parser/prompt.ts
- Library/types: packages/react-lang/src/library.ts

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A component definition.
Equivalent to TS `DefinedComponent`from`defineComponent()`.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentGroup.html)- Group
- A logical group of components for prompt organization.
- [Library](https://docs.rs/struct.Library.html)
- The full component library definition.
- [Prompt](https://docs.rs/struct.PromptOptions.html)- Options
- Options for customizing the generated prompt.
- [PropDef](https://docs.rs/struct.PropDef.html)
- A single prop/argument definition for a component.
Maps to a key in the TypeScript Zod schema’s `.shape`.

# athena_pipelines - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/athena-pipelines/3.26.3/athena_pipelines/

## Expand description

Portable Athena pipeline contracts and request-domain helpers.

This crate owns the declarative pipeline model that can be shared across the
server runtime, admin APIs, CLI/bootstrap loading, and future adapters
without depending on Actix or `AppState`.

The current scope covers:

- source/transform/sink pipeline DTOs,
- pipeline request payloads and template summaries,
- persisted template DTOs and record-to-runtime conversion helpers,
- pipeline template SQL adapters and step-log persistence helpers,
- request-independent pipeline execution orchestration behind runtime traits,
- database-backed template catalog loaders and list response contracts,
- YAML registry loading for named pipelines,
- validation and template/override resolution,
- template-name normalization and boot-template shadow policy helpers,
- gateway fetch-body construction and row alias rewriting.
- pipeline execution response contracts shared by runtime handlers and tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.ConditionEntry.html)- Entry
- A single equality condition in pipeline source configuration.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineDefinition.html)- Definition
- Full declarative pipeline definition used by templates and request merging.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineExecutionError.html)- Execution - Error
- Serializable per-row sink error returned from pipeline execution routes.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineExecutionResponse.html)- Execution - Response
- Serializable success envelope returned from `/pipelines`and`/pipelines/simulate`.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineFetchFailure.html)- Fetch - Failure
- Structured source-fetch failure returned by the runtime adapter.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineRequest.html)- Request
- Pipeline execution request with an optional named template and inline overrides.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineRunContext.html)- RunContext
- Runtime context needed by the portable pipeline runner.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineRunFetchFailure.html)- RunFetch - Failure
- Failed pipeline-run result when the source fetch cannot complete.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineRunSuccess.html)- RunSuccess
- Successful pipeline-run result returned by the portable runner.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineStepLogEntry.html)- Step - LogEntry
- One pipeline step-log row emitted for the `source`,`transform`, or`sink`stage.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineTemplateCandidate.html)- Template - Candidate
- Portable template candidate used when merging runtime-managed templates with boot registry entries.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineTemplateListResponse.html)- Template - List - Response
- Response envelope returned by `GET /pipelines/templates`.

- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineTemplateSummary.html)- Template - Summary

- Result of merging boot templates with runtime-provided templates.

- Request body for saving a managed pipeline template through admin surfaces.

- Source stage configuration for Athena pipelines.

# radsym - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/radsym/0.4.0/radsym/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#radsym)radsym

Radial symmetry detection library: center proposal generation, local circular and elliptical support analysis, support scoring, and local image-space refinement. CPU-first, deterministic, composable tools.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

The one-call [ detect_circles](https://docs.rs/pipeline/fn.detect_circles.html) runs the whole propose-score-refine
pipeline. Configure it with the

[builder:](https://docs.rs/pipeline/struct.DetectCirclesConfig.html#method.for_radii)

`DetectCirclesConfig::for_radii````
use radsym::{detect_circles, DetectCirclesConfig, ImageView, Polarity};
// 1. Load or create an image (here: synthetic bright disk)
let size = 64;
let mut data = vec![0u8; size * size];
for y in 0..size {
    for x in 0..size {
        let dx = x as f32 - 32.0;
        let dy = y as f32 - 32.0;
        if (dx * dx + dy * dy).sqrt() <= 10.0 {
            data[y * size + x] = 255;
        }
    }
}
let image = ImageView::from_slice(&data, size, size).unwrap();
// 2. Detect circles in a single call.
let config = DetectCirclesConfig::for_radii([9, 10, 11])
    .polarity(Polarity::Bright)
    .radius_hint(10.0)
    .min_score(0.2);
let detections = detect_circles(&image, &config).unwrap();
// 3. Inspect the results (sorted by descending support score).
for detection in &detections {
    println!(
        "center=({:.1}, {:.1}) r={:.1} score={:.3}",
        detection.hypothesis.center.x,
        detection.hypothesis.center.y,
        detection.hypothesis.radius,
        detection.score.total,
    );
}
assert!(!detections.is_empty());
```
Power users can still drive the propose-score-refine stages directly with
[ compute_gradient](https://docs.rs/core/gradient/fn.compute_gradient.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/propose/frst/fn.frst_response.html)

`frst_response`[,](https://docs.rs/propose/extract/fn.extract_proposals.html)

`extract_proposals`[, and](https://docs.rs/support/score/fn.score_circle_support.html)

`score_circle_support`[. To inspect why proposals were accepted or rejected, use](https://docs.rs/refine/circle/fn.refine_circle.html)

`refine_circle`[.](https://docs.rs/pipeline/fn.detect_circles_with_diagnostics.html)

`detect_circles_with_diagnostics`[§](https://docs.rs#modules)Modules

- `core`
- `propose`
- `support`
- `refine`
- `diagnostics`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

- `rayon`— parallel execution for multi-radius proposals
- `image-io`— load images via the- `image`crate
- `tracing`— structured logging
- `affine`— experimental affine-aware extensions (GFRS)
- `serde`— serialization support

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::core::coords::`- [PixelCoord](https://docs.rs/core/coords/type.PixelCoord.html);
- `pub use crate::core::error::`- [RadSymError](https://docs.rs/core/error/enum.RadSymError.html);
- `pub use crate::core::error::`- [Result](https://docs.rs/core/error/type.Result.html);

# reqwest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reqwest/^0.12/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#reqwest)reqwest

The `reqwest` crate provides a convenient, higher-level HTTP
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html).

It handles many of the things that most people just expect an HTTP client to do for them.

- Async and [blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)Clients
- Plain bodies, [JSON](https://docs.rs#json),[urlencoded](https://docs.rs#forms),[multipart](https://docs.rs/multipart/index.html)
- Customizable [redirect policy](https://docs.rs#redirect-policies)
- HTTP [Proxies](https://docs.rs#proxies)
- Uses [TLS](https://docs.rs#tls)by default
- Cookies

The [ reqwest::Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) is asynchronous (requiring Tokio). For
applications wishing  to only make a few HTTP requests, the

[API may be more convenient.](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)

`reqwest::blocking`Additional learning resources include:

[§](https://docs.rs#commercial-support)Commercial Support

For private advice, support, reviews, access to the maintainer, and the
like, reach out for [commercial support](https://seanmonstar.com/sponsor).

[§](https://docs.rs#making-a-get-request)Making a GET request

For a single request, you can use the [ get](https://docs.rs/fn.get.html) shortcut method.

```
let body = reqwest::get("https://www.rust-lang.org")
    .await?
    .text()
    .await?;
println!("body = {body:?}");
```
**NOTE**: If you plan to perform multiple requests, it is best to create a
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) and reuse it, taking advantage of keep-alive connection
pooling.

[§](https://docs.rs#making-post-requests-or-setting-request-bodies)Making POST requests (or setting request bodies)

There are several ways you can set the body of a request. The basic one is
by using the `body()` method of a [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html). This lets you set the
exact raw bytes of what the body should be. It accepts various types,
including

`String` and `Vec<u8>`. If you wish to pass a custom
type, you can use the `reqwest::Body` constructors.```
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .body("the exact body that is sent")
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#forms)Forms

It’s very common to want to send form data in a request body. This can be done with any type that can be serialized into form data.

This can be an array of tuples, or a `HashMap`, or a custom type that
implements [ Serialize](http://serde.rs).

```
// This will POST a body of `foo=bar&baz=quux`
let params = [("foo", "bar"), ("baz", "quux")];
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .form(¶ms)
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#json)JSON

There is also a `json` method helper on the [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html) that works in
a similar fashion the

`form` method. It can take any value that can be
serialized into JSON. The feature `json` is required.```
// This will POST a body of `{"lang":"rust","body":"json"}`
let mut map = HashMap::new();
map.insert("lang", "rust");
map.insert("body", "json");
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .json(&map)
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#redirect-policies)Redirect Policies

By default, a `Client` will automatically handle HTTP redirects, having a
maximum redirect chain of 10 hops. To customize this behavior, a
[ redirect::Policy](https://docs.rs/redirect/index.html) can be used with a

`ClientBuilder`.[§](https://docs.rs#cookies)Cookies

The automatic storing and sending of session cookies can be enabled with
the [ cookie_store](https://docs.rs/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.cookie_store) method on

`ClientBuilder`.[§](https://docs.rs#proxies)Proxies

**NOTE**: System proxies are enabled by default.

System proxies look in environment variables to set HTTP or HTTPS proxies.

`HTTP_PROXY` or `http_proxy` provide HTTP proxies for HTTP connections while
`HTTPS_PROXY` or `https_proxy` provide HTTPS proxies for HTTPS connections.
`ALL_PROXY` or `all_proxy` provide proxies for both HTTP and HTTPS connections.
If both the all proxy and HTTP or HTTPS proxy variables are set the more specific
HTTP or HTTPS proxies take precedence.

These can be overwritten by adding a [ Proxy](https://docs.rs/struct.Proxy.html) to

`ClientBuilder`
i.e. `let proxy = reqwest::Proxy::http("https://secure.example")?;`
or disabled by calling `ClientBuilder::no_proxy()`.`socks` feature is required if you have configured socks proxy like this:

`export https_proxy=socks5://127.0.0.1:1086`[§](https://docs.rs#tls)TLS

A `Client` will use transport layer security (TLS) by default to connect to
HTTPS destinations.

- Additional server certificates can be configured on a `ClientBuilder`with the`Certificate`
- Client certificates can be added to a `ClientBuilder`with the`Identity`
- Various parts of TLS can also be configured or even disabled on the
`ClientBuilder`.

See more details in the [ tls](https://docs.rs/tls/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm)WASM

The Client implementation automatically switches to the WASM one when the target_arch is wasm32,
the usage is basically the same as the async api. Some of the features are disabled in wasm
: [ tls](https://docs.rs/tls/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/cookie/index.html)

`cookie`[, as well as various](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)

`blocking``ClientBuilder` methods such as `timeout()` and `connector_layer()`.TLS and cookies are provided through the browser environment, so reqwest can issue TLS requests with cookies, but has limited configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

The following are a list of [Cargo features](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) that can be
enabled or disabled:

- **http2**- *(enabled by default)*: Enables HTTP/2 support.
- **default-tls**- *(enabled by default)*: Provides TLS support to connect over HTTPS.
- **native-tls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `native-tls`.
- **native-tls-vendored**: Enables the- `vendored`feature of- `native-tls`.
- **native-tls-alpn**: Enables the- `alpn`feature of- `native-tls`.
- **rustls-tls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`. Equivalent to- `rustls-tls-webpki-roots`.
- **rustls-tls-manual-roots**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`, without setting any root certificates. Roots have to be specified manually.
- **rustls-tls-webpki-roots**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`, while using root certificates from the- `webpki-roots`crate.
- **rustls-tls-native-roots**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`, while using root certificates from the- `rustls-native-certs`crate.
- **blocking**: Provides the- [blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)client API.
- **charset**- *(enabled by default)*: Improved support for decoding text.
- **cookies**: Provides cookie session support.
- **gzip**: Provides response body gzip decompression.
- **brotli**: Provides response body brotli decompression.
- **zstd**: Provides response body zstd decompression.
- **deflate**: Provides response body deflate decompression.
- **json**: Provides serialization and deserialization for JSON bodies.
- **multipart**: Provides functionality for multipart forms.
- **stream**: Adds support for- `futures::Stream`.
- **socks**: Provides SOCKS5 proxy support.
- **hickory-dns**: Enables a hickory-dns async resolver instead of default threadpool using- `getaddrinfo`.
- **system-proxy**- *(enabled by default)*: Use Windows and macOS system proxy settings automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable Features

Some feature flags require additional opt-in by the application, by setting
a `reqwest_unstable` flag.

- **http3**- *(unstable)*: Enables support for sending HTTP/3 requests.

These features are unstable, and experimental. Details about them may be changed in patch releases.

You can pass such a flag to the compiler via `.cargo/config`, or
environment variables, such as:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg reqwest_unstable" cargo build`[§](https://docs.rs#sponsors)Sponsors

Support this project by becoming a [sponsor](https://seanmonstar.com/sponsor).

- Shortcut method to quickly make a `GET`request.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`alias where the`Err`case is`reqwest::Error`.

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Deserialize JSON data to a Rust data structure.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- When serializing or deserializing JSON goes wrong.
- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- A map of String to serde_json::Value.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)- `std`
- Serialize a Rust data structure into JSON data.
- [value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html)
- The Value enum, a loosely typed way of representing any valid JSON value.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [json](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html)
- Construct a `serde_json::Value`from a JSON literal.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Deserializer.html)
- A structure that deserializes JSON into Rust values.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- This type represents all possible errors that can occur when serializing or deserializing JSON data.
- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- Represents a JSON key/value type.
- [Number](https://docs.rs/struct.Number.html)
- Represents a JSON number, whether integer or floating point.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html)- `std`
- A structure for serializing Rust values into JSON.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamDeserializer.html)- Deserializer
- Iterator that deserializes a stream into multiple JSON values.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html)
- Represents any valid JSON value.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)- reader - `std`
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from an I/O stream of JSON.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)- slice
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from bytes of JSON text.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html)- str
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from a string of JSON text.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_value.html)- value
- Interpret a `serde_json::Value`as an instance of type`T`.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html)- string - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a String of JSON.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string_pretty.html)- string_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a pretty-printed String of JSON.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_value.html)- value
- Convert a `T`into`serde_json::Value`which is an enum that can represent any valid JSON data.
- [to_vec](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)- `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a JSON byte vector.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec_pretty.html)- vec_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a pretty-printed JSON byte vector.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)- writer - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as JSON into the I/O stream.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer_pretty.html)- writer_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as pretty-printed JSON into the I/O stream.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- Alias for a `Result`with the error type`serde_json::Error`.

[64](#64)                .and_then(|r| r.json::<serde_json::Value>())
[65](#65)            {
[66](#66)                Ok(resp) => {
[67](#67)                    let data = resp.get("data").and_then(|d| d.get("data"));
[68](#68)                    if let Some(data) = data {
[69](#69)                        let field_key = field.unwrap_or("value");
[70](#70)                        if let Some(v) = data.get(field_key) {
[71](#71)                            results.insert(ref_.clone(), v.clone());
[72](#72)                        }
[73](#73)                    }
[74](#74)                }
[75](#75)                Err(_) => {}
[76](#76)            }
[77](#77)        }
[78](#78)        Ok(results)
[79](#79)    }
[80](#80)
[81](#81)    fn get(&self, reference: &str) -> Result<Option<Value>, CnosError> {
[82](#82)        let results = self.batch_get(&[reference.to_string()])?;
[83](#83)        Ok(results.into_values().next())
[84](#84)    }
[85](#85)}
[86](#86)
[87](#87)trait OrElseIfEmpty {
[88](#88)    fn or_else_if_empty<F: FnOnce() -> Option<String>>(self, f: F) -> Option<String>;
[89](#89)}
[90](#90)
[91](#91)impl OrElseIfEmpty for String {
[92](#92)    fn or_else_if_empty<F: FnOnce() -> Option<String>>(self, f: F) -> Option<String> {
[93](#93)        if self.is_empty() { f() } else { Some(self) }
[94](#94)    }
[95](#95)}
